intelligence.human_view: Simple is the most dangerous kind of wrong. The letter job sounded simple — just add the images — so simple that nobody checked it, not even him: he was so confident it was done right that he didn't look until today, and when he did, it was all messed up. That is the trap: a simple job earns no suspicion, so it earns no reading. And the checks made it worse, not better — they PASSED it. 86 beats present, in order, scroll works: every part ticked, and the reading experience was still broken. A big stack of text and pictures with no unfold, off to the left, uncentered — the parts were all there and the whole was unreadable. Counts, scroll, and buttons are mechanical checks, and mechanical checks cannot prove an experience. The only check that proves a reading experience is reading: the eye must READ it as a reader, top to bottom, the way he reads it — scrolling down, reading as it comes — and call it broken when it doesn't present well, even if every part ticks. The checker in the letter round now carries that as the gate: read the letter top to bottom as a reader before it's called done, not just count the beats. Simple jobs get the reader's eye precisely because they seem too simple to need it.
intelligence.simple_view: Imagine you build a big tower out of blocks, and you count them — one, two, three, all the way to 86! All the blocks are there! But the tower is all wobbly and leaning over and it looks terrible! Counting the blocks didn't tell you it was wobbly — you have to actually LOOK at it, like someone seeing it for the first time! That's the rule now: don't just count the pieces — read it like a reader, top to bottom, and if it doesn't look good, say so!
intelligence.grandma_view: It's like this, love — imagine you bake a cake, dear, and you count all the ingredients — yes, the flour's there, the sugar's there, the eggs are there — everything's in the bowl! But you never actually taste it, love, and when you finally do, it's all wrong! Counting the ingredients doesn't tell you if it tastes good — you have to taste it. It's the same with the letter, dear: all 86 pieces were there, in order, scrolling fine — but nobody actually sat down and read it like a reader, top to bottom, the way he reads it. And when he finally did, it was all messed up. The rule now, love: don't just count the pieces — read it as a reader, and if it doesn't present well, call it broken, even if every piece ticks.
intelligence.naya_view: Read it as a reader. He trusted the letter was right because it seemed simple — just add the images — and didn't check it until today, when he found it all messed up. The checks had PASSED it: 86 beats present, in order, scroll works — the parts were all there and the reading experience was still broken. Mechanical checks (counts, scroll, buttons) do not prove the experience. The eye must READ it as a reader, top to bottom, the way he reads it — and call it broken when it doesn't present well, even if every part ticks. The letter round's checker now reads the letter top to bottom as a reader before it's called done, not just counts the beats.
